topic: Day 1 · Fluids in AKI — Resuscitation, the U-Curve & De-resuscitation
speakerTitle: Consultant in Intensive Care Medicine & Nephrology
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Critical Care Unit
speakerBio: Dual-trained intensivist-nephrologist who runs the unit's POCUS and VExUS teaching programme and campaigns against the standing 'renal protection' fluid order she blames for more congestion than any disease.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 64-year-old woman with septic AKI arrived oliguric and hypotensive. The admitting team, following an old reflex, gave her four litres of 0.9% saline in six hours "to protect the kidneys." Twelve hours later she is puffy, her JVP is up to the earlobe, she has bibasal crackles, her oxygen requirement has doubled — and her creatinine is higher, not lower, than on admission. She was under-resuscitated at hour zero and is now drowning at hour twelve, and the chloride load she received has done her kidneys no favours at all. This is the paradox at the heart of fluids in AKI: too little fluid harms the kidney, and so does too much. The art is knowing where on the curve your patient sits — and knowing when to stop giving fluid and start taking it off.

1 · 📉 The J/U-shaped fluid–outcome curve

Forget the idea that fluid is uniformly renoprotective. The relationship between fluid balance and renal (and overall) outcome is a U- (or J-) shaped curve: mortality and AKI are worst at both ends of the fluid spectrum, and best in a middle zone of euvolaemia.

Position on curveRenal insultMechanism
Hypovolaemia (left limb)Pre-renal ischaemia → ATNLow renal perfusion pressure, reduced GFR, tubular ischaemia
Euvolaemia (trough)Best outcomesAdequate perfusion without congestion
Fluid overload (right limb)Renal venous congestion → worse AKIRaised central venous pressure transmitted back to the kidney
Both dehydration and drowning damage the kidney. Fluid is a drug with a therapeutic window — under-dose and over-dose both kill nephrons.
🎯 Renal venous congestion — the WHY of the right limb

The kidney is encapsulated, so its perfusion depends on the pressure gradient across it: renal perfusion = mean arterial pressure − central venous pressure. Pour in too much fluid and the CVP climbs; that back-pressure is transmitted through the renal vein into the encapsulated kidney, raising interstitial pressure, collapsing the peritubular capillaries and reducing GFR. So a fluid-overloaded patient can have a perfectly good blood pressure and cardiac output and still be making their AKI worse — because the problem is venous congestion, not arterial supply. This is why 'give more fluid to improve the kidneys' fails on the right limb: you are raising the very pressure that is strangling the organ.

2 · 🔀 The two questions before every bolus

Before any fluid, answer two things: (1) is the patient fluid-responsive (will a bolus actually increase cardiac output)? and (2) is there room for the fluid, or is the patient already congested? A patient can be fluid-responsive and congested at the same time — and then fluid is the wrong answer.

💡 Only about half of haemodynamically unstable patients are fluid-responsive

Roughly 50% of critically ill patients given a fluid bolus do not increase their cardiac output — the fluid simply leaks into the interstitium and adds to congestion. Static measures (a single CVP, "the JVP looks low") are poor predictors. Use dynamic assessments of responsiveness instead, and re-assess after every bolus rather than committing to a fixed prescription.

3 · 🦵 Assessing fluid responsiveness — dynamic, not static

TestWhat it doesPositive =
Passive leg raise (PLR)Tilts ~300 mL of venous blood from the legs into the central circulation — a reversible, endogenous fluid challengeStroke volume / cardiac output rises ~≥10% → fluid-responsive. Reversible, gives no actual fluid.
Stroke volume variation / pulse pressure variationHeart–lung interaction on positive-pressure ventilationVariation >~12–13% (caveats: sinus rhythm, controlled ventilation, adequate tidal volumes)
POCUS — IVCDiameter and collapsibility/distensibility with respirationSmall, highly collapsible IVC suggests responsiveness; a plethoric, non-collapsing IVC suggests congestion
Fluid challenge with re-assessmentSmall aliquot (e.g. 250 mL) then re-measureCardiac output rises → responsive. If not, STOP.

VExUS — grading venous congestion

The Venous Excess Ultrasound (VExUS) score is the mirror-image of responsiveness assessment: instead of asking "can I give fluid?" it asks "have I given too much?" It combines the IVC diameter with Doppler waveforms of the hepatic vein, portal vein and intrarenal veins to grade systemic venous congestion (0 to 3). A high VExUS grade — particularly a pulsatile portal vein and a discontinuous/monophasic intrarenal venous pattern — indicates congestion severe enough to be harming the kidney, and is a signal to de-resuscitate, not to give more.

🎯 Responsiveness and tolerance are two different questions

PLR/SVV/IVC-collapsibility tell you whether a bolus will raise cardiac output. VExUS and clinical congestion tell you whether the patient can tolerate that fluid without being harmed. Give fluid only when the answer to both is favourable: responsive AND uncongested. A responsive but congested patient needs their cardiac output supported some other way (vasopressor, inotrope), not more litres.

4 · 🧪 Which fluid — balanced crystalloid vs 0.9% saline

"Normal" saline is a misnomer: 0.9% NaCl contains 154 mmol/L of chloride — far above the plasma level of ~100 — and no other buffer. Large volumes cause a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, and supraphysiological chloride triggers renal afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, reducing renal blood flow and GFR. Balanced solutions (Hartmann's/lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte) have near-physiological chloride and a bicarbonate-precursor buffer.

0.9% "normal" salineBalanced crystalloid (Hartmann's / Plasma-Lyte)
Chloride154 mmol/L (supraphysiological)~98–111 mmol/L (physiological)
BufferNoneLactate / acetate / gluconate → bicarbonate
Acid–base effectHyperchloraemic metabolic acidosisNeutral
Renal blood flowChloride-driven afferent vasoconstriction ↓ RBFPreserved
CaveatPreferred in hypochloraemic alkalosis, some hyponatraemia, and TBI (avoid hypotonic)Mild hypotonicity/potassium content — caution in severe hyperkalaemia debated (small K load)

The trial evidence

  • SMART (2018) — ~15,000 ICU patients: balanced crystalloids reduced the composite of death, new renal-replacement therapy or persistent renal dysfunction ("major adverse kidney events at 30 days", MAKE30) versus saline. A modest but real signal favouring balanced fluids.
  • SALT-ED (2018) — non-critically-ill ED patients: fewer major adverse kidney events with balanced fluids.
  • BaSICS (2021) and PLUS (2022) — large ICU trials that did not show a clear mortality difference, tempering the effect size. The overall picture: balanced solutions are at least as safe as saline and probably modestly better for the kidney, so they are the sensible default for large-volume resuscitation, while saline retains specific niches.
Make balanced crystalloid your default resuscitation fluid. "Normal" saline is neither normal nor kidney-neutral — its chloride load acidifies the blood and constricts the renal afferent arteriole.
⚠️ Against starches — the fluid that caused the harm it was meant to prevent

Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) colloids were once marketed as volume-sparing resuscitation fluids. The VISEP, 6S and CHEST trials showed the opposite: starches increased the need for renal-replacement therapy and, in sepsis, increased mortality — the molecules are taken up by and injure the renal tubules. Starches are now contraindicated in critically ill and septic patients. Do not use HES for resuscitation in AKI or sepsis, ever. Albumin has niche roles (e.g. spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome, large-volume paracentesis) but is not a first-line resuscitation fluid for undifferentiated AKI.

5 · 🚫 Diuretics do NOT treat AKI

This is one of the most persistent errors on the acute take: reaching for furosemide to "kick-start the kidneys" or "convert oliguric to non-oliguric AKI." The evidence is unambiguous — diuretics do not prevent AKI, do not treat established AKI, do not hasten renal recovery, and do not reduce the need for dialysis or death. KDIGO explicitly recommends against using diuretics to treat AKI (other than to manage volume overload).

  • Furosemide converts oliguria to a larger urine output in some patients, but this is cosmetic — it makes the chart look better without improving the kidney, and can lull the team into thinking the AKI is improving.
  • Chasing diuresis with escalating furosemide risks hypovolaemia (tipping the patient back onto the harmful left limb of the curve), ototoxicity at high doses, and electrolyte derangement.
  • The only legitimate role of diuretics in AKI is to manage fluid overload in a patient who is still making urine — i.e. to move a congested patient back toward the trough of the curve. That is symptomatic management of volume, not treatment of the kidney injury itself.
Diuretics treat fluid overload, not kidney injury. A bigger urine output is not a better kidney — do not mistake the chart improving for the patient improving.

6 · 🌊 De-resuscitation — the phase everyone forgets

Resuscitation and de-resuscitation are two distinct phases of critical illness. Early shock needs prompt, adequate fluid to restore perfusion. But once the patient is stable and no longer fluid-responsive, accumulated positive fluid balance becomes an active toxin — a persistently positive cumulative balance is one of the strongest predictors of death and non-recovery of renal function in AKI. The de-resuscitation phase deliberately removes that accumulated fluid.

  • Stop maintenance fluids the moment the patient is drinking or fed and euvolaemic — "creeping" maintenance and drug-diluent volumes silently accumulate litres.
  • Actively remove fluid once stable and congested: diuretics (here they are appropriate — for volume, not for the kidney) or ultrafiltration/RRT if diuretic-resistant.
  • Target a neutral-to-negative cumulative balance guided by weights, examination and congestion assessment (VExUS/POCUS).
  • Conceptualise fluid therapy in four phases — Resuscitation → Optimisation → Stabilisation → Evacuation (the ROSE model) — and know which phase your patient is in before you write a fluid order.
🎯 Congestion vs hypovolaemia — the bedside contrast

Hypovolaemia: cool peripheries, tachycardia, low/collapsing IVC, responsive to PLR, dry axillae, low urine with high urine osmolality. → Give balanced crystalloid, re-assess after each bolus. Congestion: raised JVP, plethoric non-collapsing IVC, high VExUS grade, crackles/oedema, worsening oxygenation, rising creatinine despite a good blood pressure. → Stop fluids and de-resuscitate. The same rising creatinine can mean opposite things at the two ends of the curve — which is why you assess volume status directly rather than reflexively giving fluid.

7 · 🧑‍⚕️ M&M — drowned in the name of the kidneys

☠️ Mortality & Morbidity — the four litres that made it worse

Return to our opening patient. A 64-year-old with septic AKI was given four litres of 0.9% saline in six hours under a blanket "renal protection" order, with no reassessment of fluid responsiveness after the first bolus. By hour twelve she had a raised JVP, bibasal crackles, an oxygen requirement that had doubled, a new hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis — and a higher creatinine. She had become fluid-unresponsive and congested: the extra litres were sitting in her lungs and back-pressuring her kidneys (renal venous congestion), while the chloride load acidified her and constricted her afferent arterioles. She required non-invasive ventilation and, ultimately, ultrafiltration to remove the fluid. Lessons: (1) fluid is a drug with a U-shaped dose–response — 'give fluid for the kidneys' is not a strategy; (2) reassess responsiveness (PLR/POCUS) after every bolus rather than committing to a fixed volume; (3) use balanced crystalloid, not chloride-rich saline, for large-volume resuscitation; (4) recognise the switch from resuscitation to de-resuscitation early — the positive balance that saved her at hour zero was drowning her by hour twelve. She was under-resuscitated, then over-resuscitated, and never right-resuscitated.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. The fluid–outcome curve is U-shaped: both hypovolaemia and fluid overload harm the kidney. Aim for the euvolaemic trough.
  2. Fluid overload harms via renal venous congestion — high CVP is transmitted back into the encapsulated kidney, collapsing peritubular capillaries and lowering GFR even with a good blood pressure.
  3. Assess responsiveness dynamically (passive leg raise, SVV/PPV, POCUS/IVC) and tolerance/congestion (VExUS) — give fluid only when responsive and uncongested, re-assessing after every bolus.
  4. Balanced crystalloid is the default (SMART, SALT-ED); 0.9% saline's chloride load causes hyperchloraemic acidosis and afferent vasoconstriction. Reserve saline for specific niches.
  5. No starches in AKI/sepsis (6S, CHEST, VISEP — more RRT and death); albumin has niche uses only.
  6. Diuretics do not treat AKI — no renoprotection, no faster recovery, no fewer deaths (KDIGO). Their only role is managing fluid overload in a patient still making urine.
  7. De-resuscitate once stable: a persistently positive cumulative balance predicts death and non-recovery — stop maintenance fluids and actively remove accumulated volume (ROSE model).

moderatorQs.q: Explain mechanistically why giving more fluid to a fluid-overloaded patient can worsen their AKI even when their blood pressure and cardiac output are good.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because renal perfusion depends on the pressure gradient across the kidney, roughly mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure, and the kidney is encapsulated. Over-filling raises the CVP, and that venous back-pressure is transmitted through the renal vein into the rigid renal capsule, raising interstitial pressure, collapsing the peritubular capillaries and reducing GFR — this is renal venous congestion. So the injury on the right limb of the U-shaped curve is a venous outflow problem, not an arterial supply one, which is why a patient with a perfectly adequate blood pressure and cardiac output can still have their AKI driven worse by additional fluid. The correct response to a congested, responsive patient is to support the circulation by another route and to de-resuscitate, not to give more litres.

moderatorQs.q: Summarise the trial evidence on balanced crystalloids versus 0.9% saline and what your default resuscitation fluid should be.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: 0.9% saline delivers a supraphysiological 154 mmol/L of chloride, causing hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and chloride-mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction that reduces renal blood flow. SMART (~15,000 ICU patients) and SALT-ED (ED patients) both showed fewer major adverse kidney events at 30 days with balanced crystalloids, while the larger BaSICS and PLUS trials did not show a clear mortality difference — so the effect is modest but consistently favours balanced fluids for the kidney and never favours saline. The sensible position: make balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's/Plasma-Lyte) the default for large-volume resuscitation, reserving 0.9% saline for specific niches such as hypochloraemic alkalosis, some hyponatraemias and traumatic brain injury (avoiding hypotonicity). And never use hydroxyethyl starch — 6S, CHEST and VISEP showed more renal-replacement therapy and death.

moderatorQs.q: A colleague wants to give furosemide to 'kick-start' an oliguric AKI. What does the evidence say and what is the only legitimate role for diuretics here?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The evidence is clear and KDIGO recommends against it: diuretics do not prevent AKI, do not treat established AKI, do not accelerate renal recovery, and do not reduce the need for dialysis or death. Converting an oliguric to a non-oliguric picture with furosemide is cosmetic — it improves the fluid chart without improving the kidney, and it risks lulling the team while causing hypovolaemia (pushing the patient back onto the harmful left limb of the curve), ototoxicity and electrolyte loss. The only legitimate role for diuretics in AKI is to manage fluid overload in a patient who is still making urine — moving a congested patient back toward euvolaemia — which is treatment of volume status, not of the kidney injury itself.

audienceQs.q: How do I actually decide at the bedside whether to give a fluid bolus or start de-resuscitating?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Answer two separate questions. First, is the patient fluid-responsive — will a bolus raise cardiac output? Use a passive leg raise (a reversible ~300 mL auto-transfusion; a ≥10% rise in stroke volume is positive), stroke-volume/pulse-pressure variation on the ventilator, or a small 250 mL challenge with re-measurement — remembering only about half of unstable patients are responsive. Second, can they tolerate it — use POCUS/IVC and the VExUS score for venous congestion. Give fluid only if responsive AND uncongested. If they are congested (raised JVP, plethoric IVC, high VExUS, worsening oxygenation, rising creatinine despite good blood pressure), stop fluids and de-resuscitate — support the circulation by another route and actively remove accumulated volume.

audienceQs.q: Why is 0.9% sodium chloride called 'normal' saline if it's bad for the kidneys, and when is it still the right choice?
audienceQs.answerHTML: 'Normal' is a historical label, not a physiological one — 0.9% saline contains 154 mmol/L of chloride against a plasma level of about 100, with no buffer. In large volumes that chloride load causes a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and constricts the renal afferent arteriole, reducing renal blood flow, which is why balanced crystalloids are the better default. Saline is still the right choice in specific situations: hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (e.g. from vomiting/NG losses), some hyponatraemias, and in traumatic brain injury where you must avoid the relative hypotonicity of balanced solutions. So think of it as a targeted tool for particular problems, not the everyday resuscitation fluid.

audienceQs.q: The team keeps prescribing maintenance fluids on a patient who's now eating and stable with AKI. Why does that matter?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because in a stable, no-longer-fluid-responsive patient, accumulated positive balance becomes an active harm — a persistently positive cumulative fluid balance is one of the strongest predictors of death and non-recovery of renal function in AKI, driving pulmonary oedema and renal venous congestion. 'Creeping' maintenance fluids and the volume of drug diluents silently add litres. Once a patient is drinking or fed and euvolaemic, maintenance fluids should be stopped, and if they are congested the team should move into active de-resuscitation — diuretics (appropriate here, for volume) or ultrafiltration if diuretic-resistant — targeting a neutral-to-negative balance. Flagging the unnecessary maintenance prescription and reviewing diluent volumes is a genuinely renoprotective intervention.
